title: Conservation Drive subdivision approved with staff setbacks
subtitle: Community planning permit draft, Official Plan deferred sites, and early looks at Barrel Yards and Columbia Street towers.
overview: Council approved the zone change and draft plan of subdivision for 556, 560 and 576 Conservation Drive, led by Mattamy Homes. The plan includes homes, a park, an elementary school block and protected natural areas. Council kept staff's recommended setbacks and rejected an amendment that would have allowed narrower side yards, smaller front yards and larger porch and balcony projections {{vote:m4}}. The approval then carried {{vote:m5}}.

Council also directed staff to consult the public on the second draft Community Planning Permit By-law for Uptown and the Herb Street corridor, which would combine zoning, site plan and minor variance approvals into one faster process. It asked the province to adjust Official Plan Amendment 58 for four sites and to lift or keep deferrals on others.

Two early-stage developments were presented at informal public meetings, with no decisions: additional towers at the Barrel Yards in Uptown, and five towers of 37 to 41 storeys at 170 and 180 Columbia Street West. Staff will report back at later formal meetings. Residents can follow these applications and the planning permit consultation on Engage Waterloo.

decisions.detail: Council approved the zone change, draft plan of subdivision and a demolition-control extension to October 30, 2030 for replacing two dwellings, with five modified subdivision conditions {{vote:m5}}.
Council rejected an amendment that would have allowed reduced side-yard setbacks and larger front-yard balcony projections at Conservation Drive {{vote:m4}}.
Council received the report and directed staff to consult the public and interested parties on the second draft by-law and urban design guidelines.
Council asked the province to add four area-specific policies, remove deferrals on some properties, and keep deferrals on others until Phase 2 of the Official Plan Review.

debate: On Conservation Drive, staff argued that narrow side yards cause drainage and grading problems, leave no room for ladders, fences or bins, and reduce space for front-yard trees given the utility easement. Staff said Waterloo has had problems in older areas with very narrow side yards.

The applicant said the requests were about affordability, estimating roughly $40,000 in savings per home from smaller lots, and said similar standards are used in Kitchener, Cambridge and elsewhere without reported complaints. It also said its house designs would not fit staff's front setback.

Councillors supporting the amendment pointed to housing affordability as a top constituent concern. Opponents cited precedent, long-term drainage risk and the impact on additional dwelling units. They also doubted the affordability benefit for detached homes and suggested a city-wide review of side-yard standards.

On the planning permit system, one councillor questioned whether residents would learn how their comments were used, given no mail-out for class 2 applications and no separate public meeting for class 3. Staff pointed to signs, website postings, earlier mailings to nearby owners, and said council notification of variations would be considered.

At the informal meetings, councillors asked about flood risk, traffic at Columbia and Phillip, tower separation, a 9-metre rail setback against the 15 metres required, and affordable units. Staff and applicants said studies were under review.
